query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A high‐temperature pre‐oxidation treatment that deliberately forms a thin, adherent Al2O3 passivation layer on the surface of boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by acting as a diffusion barrier to Al infiltration and aggressive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Boronide-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, having their native surface without a deliberately engineered protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Subject the components to a controlled high-temperature pre-oxidation process (in an oxidizing atmosphere) to form a continuous, dense alumina (Al2O3) layer on the boride surface prior to exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.conditions: The pre-formed Al2O3 layer must remain adherent and intact under plating conditions (typically around 700–800 °C) and during exposure times relevant to hot-dip processes in aluminum plating equipment.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform Al2O3 film at the surface which modifies the surface chemistry and microstructure by providing a chemically stable barrier.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 passivation layer, being thermodynamically stable and dense, slows down the dissolution and interfacial reaction between the molten aluminum and the underlying boride phase. This barrier limits aluminum penetration and minimizes the corrosion-mediated degradation of the component.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated boride surfaces, the pre-oxidized components will show a significant reduction in weight loss and corrosion depth when exposed to molten aluminum, indicating an improved corrosion resistance. Although the exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain, a measurable reduction in corrosion rate (e.g., a reduction in corrosion penetration area by over 20–30% under comparable test conditions) is anticipated.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with their as-received (non-pre-oxidized) surface exposed directly to molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to be effective so long as the Al2O3 layer remains continuous and adherent. Any mechanical damage or prolonged exposure that leads to spallation of the oxide scale may diminish its protective function.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal pre-oxidation parameters (temperature, time, and atmosphere) for forming an ideally protective Al2O3 layer are not fully defined, and the long-term stability of the oxide under repeated thermal cycling remains to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component samples: one set will undergo the proposed high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment to form an Al2O3 layer, while the control set will remain untreated. Both sets will then be immersed in molten aluminum under conditions simulating hot-dip plating (temperature, immersion time, and thermal cycling as in service).
measurements: Weight loss (mass change) measurement after exposure
Cross-sectional microscopic evaluation of corrosion depth and oxide layer integrity via SEM/EDS
Surface phase analysis (e.g., XRD) to verify the presence and stability of the Al2O3 layer
Comparative electrochemical corrosion tests, if applicable
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit statistically significant lower corrosion rates, reduced corrosion depths, or improved surface integrity compared to the untreated controls (or if the Al2O3 layer degrades rapidly under service conditions), the hypothesis that the pre-oxidation treatment improves corrosion resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

notes.research_context: The research group asking this question works on high-entropy (multi-principal-element) alloys for high-temperature applications.
